{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Canonical slugs to prefer: `anthropic`, `openai`, `google-deepmind`, `meta`, `xai`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `qwen`, `nvidia`, `microsoft`, `amazon`, `apple`, `threat-intel`, `cyber-offense`, `cyber-defense`, `influence-ops`, `scams-fraud`, `deepfakes`, `prompt-injection`, `agents`, `agent-security`, `alignment`, `interpretability`, `evals`, `open-weights`, `reasoning-models`, `scaling`, `compute`, `chips`, `export-controls`, `energy`, `datacenters`, `china`, `eu-ai-act`, `us-federal-policy`, `us-state-policy`, `uk`, `copyright`, `privacy`, `military`, `autonomous-weapons`, `pentagon`, `healthcare`, `fda`, `drug-discovery`, `bio-risk`, `ai-for-science`, `robotics`, `labor`, `education`, `elections`, `surveillance`, `child-safety`, `incidents`, `funding`, `earnings`. Add an entity slug (company, agency, named group) when the story is about that entity.

**Storylines** (optional; usually one, at most two): the ids from `node scripts/build.js --storylines` whose arc this item advances — a new development in *that story*, not merely the same topic. Only existing ids with status `live` or `proposed`; the validator rejects unknown or resolved ids. Omit the key when the item belongs to none. Never coin an id here.

**Impact** (optional but encouraged): `beneficial`, `harmful`, `mixed`, or `neutral` — the demonstrated effect in the story, not your prediction.

**Flags** (include every one that applies; omit the key if none): `company-claim` — a company-reported benchmark, user count, revenue or capability claim not independently verified; `single-source` — only one outlet has it; `preprint` — research not peer reviewed; `update` — a story covered in an earlier edition, with new facts only.

**Style**: plain, declarative, numbers over adjectives. Attribute claims ("Anthropic says", "the paper reports", "according to the filing"). No hype, no hedging language beyond what the sources support. British or American spelling — either, consistently.

**Absolute rules**:
- Never invent a URL, a number, a quote, a name, or a date. If unsure, open the source again.
- Never write a bullet you could not point to a sentence in the source for.
- Never link a URL you did not open in this session.
- Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and baseline. Never round, convert, or compute new figures.
- Link the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page (the validator rejects these).

{"stdout":"# Sources

The sweep list for every edition. **Primary** sources (labs, papers, governments, court filings, security vendors' own reports) are always preferred for the link beside a headline; **secondary** sources (press, newsletters, aggregators) are used to discover stories and as corroboration. Wherever a secondary source reports on a primary document, link the primary document too.

Fetch hints: `WebFetch` works on most pages below. RSS/Atom URLs are listed where they exist because they are the most reliable "what changed in the last 24h" signal.

**Refuses `WebFetch` — read with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` instead** (confirmed 11 Sep 2026; the sites have given permission for direct reads and the fetcher identifies itself. If the direct fetch returns a paywall stub or nothing usable, use `WebSearch` result text, RSS feeds where listed, or an alternative openable source, and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never archive or cache sites): Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, NYT, FT, The Information, Wired, The Verge, Ars Technica, AP, The Guardian, CNBC, Axios article pages, BleepingComputer, `openai.com/index/*` article pages (the RSS feed `openai.com/news/rss.xml` and `developers.openai.com` docs work), Data Center Dynamics article pages (index pages work), Oracle newsroom (investor.oracle.com works), x.ai, Nature (auth redirect), smol.ai (402), FDA newsroom index (401 — search for the specific press release URL instead). `WebSearch` with `allowed_domains` also rejects reuters.com, wsj.com, nytimes.com, wired.com, theverge.com, arstechnica.com, businessinsider.com — search without the domain filter and use whatever result text is visible.

Alphabet's Q3 2026 results (reported October 28, 2026) show Cloud revenue up sharply, but capex guidance was held, not raised.

- **Cloud revenue:** Google Cloud revenue rose 103% to $30.7 billion, led by strong growth in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) across enterprise AI infrastructure and enterprise AI solutions. TPU systems sales were also a meaningful contributor to revenue growth. Cloud operating income was $11.12 billion.
- **Total revenue:** Consolidated revenue was $127.6 billion, up 25%, though it missed expectations. CNBC reported it was the company's first top-and-bottom-line miss in nearly four years.
- **Capex:** Q3 capital expenditures were $51.36 billion in Q3, falling short of the $55.09 billion expected by analysts. On guidance, the full-year 2026 CapEx guidance range of $195 to $205 billion remains unchanged. CNBC noted Alphabet maintained its full-year capex forecast after lifting guidance to between $195 billion and $205 billion during Q2. So the raise happened in Q2, not Q3.
- **Free cash flow:** Third quarter free cash flow was negative $9.065 billion. Alphabet also said 2027 expected to increase significantly from 2026 levels.
- **EPS:** Sources differ. CNBC cites $2.67 adjusted EPS, while Constellation Research reports net income of $26.17 billion, or $2.12 a share.

Volt Typhoon hides zero-day attacks using 'Silent Train' framework

- Home

- Volt Typhoon hides zero-day attacks using 'Silent Train' framework

# Volt Typhoon hides zero-day attacks using 'Silent Train' framework

By

# Bill Toulas

- October 28, 2026

- 12:00 PM

- 0



Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon has been using a framework that relies on rotating chains of connected devices compromised on demand, including for zero-day attacks targeting high-value systems.


The framework has been dubbed Silent Train because the threat actor uses it against select targets, cleans it up after each operation, and refreshes it continuously.


Researchers at Black Lotus Labs, the threat research division of communications company Lumen, have been tracking Silent Train for three years and confirmed that Volt Typhoon exploited at least four zero-day vulnerabilities in attacks targeting edge and management infrastructure.


Targets include telecommunication firms, government agencies, defense contractors, educational institutes, utilities/critical infrastructure, satellite service providers, IT firms, MSPs, transportation, aviation, and emergency services.


Black Lotus Labs’ observations indicate the most targeted regions are California, Texas, and Hawaii, suggesting a focus on Indo-Pacific matters.




Victims map

Source: Black Lotus Labs





Volt Typhoon previously targeted U.S. critical infrastructure, including communications, energy, transportation, and water systems, with CISA warning that it seeks to establish access for potential disruption during a future crisis or conflict.


According to the researchers, Silent Train's deployment was partly fueled by the FBI's disruption of KV-Botnet , a botnet that Volt Typhoon used to evade detection when attacking critical infrastructure in the US.




Activity comparison over time

Source: Black Lotus Labs






# Silent Train relay network


Silent Train is practically a relay infrastructure formed of compromised devices that Volt Typhoon uses to hide the origin of its attacks.


The operators route their activity through VPS infrastructure outside the United States, then pass it through hacked devices such as routers that act as intermediate relays before launching attacks.


Black Lotus Labs says Intelbras modems served as overseas relays, while Netgear Orbi devices acted as hops in the U.S.




Silent Train attack overview

Source: Black Lotus Labs





The threat actor's use of Silent Train involves exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, exfiltrating data, and maintaining persistent remote access to compromised systems.


By monitoring Silent Train activity, the researchers were able to observe zero-day exploits for the following products:




- CVE-2026-16812 – VeloCloudOrchestrator


- CVE-2026-20127 – Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN


- CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 – N-able N-central


- CVE-2024-39717 – Versa Director


- Quest KACE (suspected zero-day)



Compromising these platforms gives threat actors broad administrative control, enabling credential theft, remote access, and reach into downstream customers without the “noisy” lateral movement that might trigger detection.

**Title:** The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents

**Authors (20):** Weidong Tang, Ruiheng Wang, Jingxuan Zhang, Hexin Wang, Haoyuan Chen, Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Yixing Ma, Zichen Jiang, Ziyu Guo, Haodong Li, Zhengbo Jiao, Zhiqing Cui, Xinxiang Yin, Shuo Liang, Zhenglin Wan, Hongzhan Lin, Wangbo Zhao, Kaipeng Zhang, Pengfei Zhou, Odin Zhang, and Yang You. (The page lists "Wangbo Zhao Kaipeng Zhang" as a single entry, so I split them here based on the likely pairing.)

**Institutions:** The page does not list any author affiliations.

**Abstract (paraphrased):** The paper proposes The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework that couples world generation with evolution of the agent's harness through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. The authors argue that tasks with different modalities can share the same underlying capability requirements. Evolver reorganizes a task tree into a capability tree, and Creator builds simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for each shared capability. Explorer evolves reusable capability modules along that tree, forming a Harness tree. A Capability-Aware Harness Router then selects module configurations based on public task information. The evolved harnesses improve mean performance by **34 points** across **28 training benchmarks** and by **26 points** across **18 unseen benchmarks**, including **two real-world embodied tasks**.

**Submission date:** Submitted on 26 Oct 2026 (v1: Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:03:34 UTC)

**Title:** Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory

**Authors (11):** Xuan He, Sining Zhoubian, Ruozhen Yang, Yuhao Wen, Zhineng Wang, Yuyang Hu, Ke Yang, Yuyu Zhang, Ping Nie, Jiawei Han, ChengXiang Zhai

**Institutions:** Not listed on the page.

**Abstract (paraphrased):** The paper examines whether building a memory layer for long-horizon agents adds value over direct retrieval from raw history, which is still unclear. In a large-scale evaluation across several benchmarks and model backbones, the authors find that many dedicated memory systems perform worse than naive RAG, which suggests a negative net value. Using RAG as the reference, they split memory's net value into gains (memory benefit) and losses (memory tax) relative to direct retrieval. Both come from how memory reorganizes and accesses the raw information. Some of these changes, such as restructuring facts or distilling preferences, are meant to help, while others can remove or obscure evidence. Because the benefits are the intended design effects, the paper focuses on the overlooked memory tax, analyzes how it arises from both the system and the evaluation, and extends the concept to other application scenarios. The authors aim to shift attention from standalone performance toward the net value of memory, and they state they will open-source the code and results.

**Numbers:** The abstract contains no exact numerical results.

**Title:** RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback

**arXiv ID:** 2610.33624 (cs.CL; also cs.AI)

**Submission date:** 24 October 2026 (v1, 11:54:45 UTC)

**Authors (18):** Yue Huang, Yanbo Wang, Lichi Li, Yuanyuan Chen, Andreas Haupt, Xiaonan Luo, Zheyuan Liu, Jihye Choi, Felix Juefei-Xu, Xiangliang Zhang, Radha Poovendran, Misha Sra, Ying Liu, Ben Burtenshaw, Thomas Wolf, Alex Pentland, Zichen Chen, Zhangchen Xu

**Institutions:** The page does not list author affiliations, so I can't provide them from this content.

**Abstract summary:** The paper asks whether AI agents can autonomously train useful language models and improve them using user feedback. It presents RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement.

- **Setup:** Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base.
- **Stage 1 (six days):** Each agent gets 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster. Agents choose data, implement training, and select checkpoints.
- **Evaluation:** Models are tested on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations.
- **Stage 1 results:** All ten agents produced working assistants. The strongest, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closed a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating was close to NVIDIA Instruct after adjusting for answer length and formatting.
- **Stage 2:** Agents received comparison records and votes involving their Stage 1 model and three more days of training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference, eight of the ten models improved in style-adjusted relative rating.
- **Caveats:** Benchmark gains were modest and not clearly linked to preference gains. Some agents encouraged longer responses, and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT.
- **Framing:** The authors present the work as a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means.

Alphabet shares fall on Q3 revenue miss
Closing Bell: Overtime

Alphabet shares slumped more than 10% after the search giant reported a drop in free cash flow during the third quarter, in a worrying sign for the artificial intelligence trade.
Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:

- Earnings per share : $2.67 adjusted vs. $3.02 expected

- Revenue: $127.58 billion vs. $128.22 billion

Revenue grew 25% from a year ago, but the company posted its first top-and-bottom-line miss in nearly four years.
Net income fell to $26.17 billion, or $2.12 per share, down from $34.98 billion, or $2.87 per share, a year ago.
The Google parent reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion, which fell much further than the $2.70 billion expected by analysts.
As questions mount over heightened spending on the AI buildout, Alphabet's capital expenditures totaled $51.36 billion in Q3, falling short of the $55.09 billion expected by analysts. Investors are looking for a substantial return on investment to warrant the big spending plans from the hyperscalers.
Alphabet maintained its full-year capital expenditures forecast after lifting guidance to between $195 billion and $205 billion during the second quarter from $190 billion. Annual capex is expected to top $200 billion before exceeding $300 billion in 2027.

"We continue to expect our capex to increase significantly in 2027, and will provide further details on our Q4 call," finance chief Anat Ashkenazi told analysts during an earnings call.
The company's borrowing rose sharply during the quarter, with long-term debt climbing to $125.1 billion, up from $21.6 billion a year earlier — an increase of about 479%.
Operating income totaled $40.58 billion, missing a $43.19 billion forecast from FactSet.

# Read more CNBC tech news

- Amazon’s anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI

- Chart: Anthropic’s cash pile towers over nearly every U.S. company

- Google alters its cloud playbook, enlisting partners to sell more AI chips

- A guide to some of the biggest risks in Anthropic's IPO prospectus

Alphabet saw a $99.03 billion windfall in revenue from equity holdings in the second quarter, fueled by stakes in SpaceX and Anthropic . However, the category weighed on results in the third quarter, resulting in a loss of $8.66 billion.
The company continues to open its wallet to fuel the AI expansion, and that has contributed to strong revenue growth in its cloud division, home to its suite of AI offerings.
"We are seeing extraordinary demand and strong growth from both AI labs, capital markets, financial service institutions, and enterprises," said Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian in his first public earnings call remarks.
Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion, surpassing the $28.7 billion expected by analysts. The company has continued taking market share from larger rivals Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure.
The strong cloud results did little to shake off Google's largely negative print.
"The cloud business was the only business that beat at 103% growth," said Jefferies analyst Brent Thill on CNBC's Closing Bell: Overtime. "The Street wanted 100%, so it didn't beat by much, and it missed some of the high-end targets. Everything else missed."
The company's aggressive push on AI models did show signs of consumer adoption. Google said its Gemini app reached 1 billion users, making it the fastest-growing product in its history, the company said.
CEO Sundar Pichai told analysts that the company is already seeing strong demand for its recently launched Argon Gemini model. Its Carbon iteration announced on Wednesday outperforms Argon "on almost every domain," he added.
Alphabet's search revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion. That fell short of a $64.96 billion estimate. Pichai said the company's AI investments powered the highest query growth rate over the last five years.

Title:
Pricing Cross-Bank Context in Federated Anti-Money Laundering

Lidia Losavio , Dario Fenoglio , Martin Gjoreski , Marc Langheinrich

Comments:
Accepted at the ICAIF 2026 Workshop on Financial AI Security, Privacy and Safety, Milan, Italy (non-archival). 10 pages, 8 figures, 1 table

Subjects:
Cryptography and Security (cs.CR) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Most graph-based Anti-Money Laundering (AML) methods assume access to a pooled transaction graph containing all accounts and payments, which in reality does not exist. Federated learning offers the necessary privacy guarantees but it remains unclear how money laundering patterns spanning separate graphs can effectively be detected. We exploit transactions already recorded by both endpoint banks to approximate remote account states locally, enabling multi-layer Graph Neural Network (GNN) computation without additional account-specific exchange. Starting from this baseline, we test whether the remaining context is worth sharing, using a disclosure ladder that adds two transaction counts per remote account or the counterparty's own GNN states. On AMLworld HI-Small, across six GNN backbones and up to 32 silos, the observable baseline yields the largest gain and keeps it as fragmentation shrinks the visible slice; counts add a robust correction, while exact remote states help only in specific regimes. In controlled privacy--utility studies, the noise needed to protect shared states erases their detection value before it buys meaningful privacy, whereas counts stay useful even under strong privacy protection. These findings support a practical rule for banks: use what they already record, and formally protect the little that must move.

Title:
Merkle-Tree-Based Verifiable Public Data Auditing for Cloud Object Storage Using Smart Contracts

Siri Reddy Tadi , K. Gangadhara Rao , M. Venu Gopalachari , C. Chetann Reddy , Jaswanth Bhimireddy

Comments:
15 pages, 12 figures, 11 tables

Subjects:
Cryptography and Security (cs.CR) ; Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

Owners of data in cloud object storage cannot directly check whether the provider still keeps every object unchanged. Existing research mostly checks blocks inside files or relies on third-party auditors, and less attention has been given to checking each object against a public blockchain reference while measuring the cost. A full-data audit downloads every object and compares it with a saved hash list, which is slow and only as reliable as that list. We propose a public auditing system in which the SHA-256 hash of each object and its name forms a leaf of a Merkle tree, so the whole dataset is represented by one Merkle root. This root is stored in an Ethereum smart contract as a trusted public record, while the objects stay with the provider. An auditor downloads an object, rebuilds the root using a short Merkle proof and compares it with the stored root, marking the object as intact, modified or missing. In five experiments on an S3-compatible store and a local Hardhat blockchain (normal audit, single- and multiple-object tampering, deletion and scalability), the system detected 15 of 15 single modifications, 2,205 of 2,205 modified objects and 830 of 830 deleted objects with no false alarms. The proof needed only 14 hashes for 10,000 objects, so checking one object took about 10 ms and a 100-object sample about 150 ms regardless of dataset size, while a full audit of 10,000 objects (14.3 s) took about as long as downloading them (13.5 s). Storing the root cost 91,863 gas, 252 times less than storing 1,000 hashes on-chain. The system thus shows exactly which objects were modified or are missing, with its main savings coming from checking selected objects.

Title:

Yuepeng Hu , Chongyu Fan , Sirat Samyoun , Jian Du

Subjects:
Cryptography and Security (cs.CR) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

LLM agents increasingly access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), but the natural-language metadata used to describe those tools creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this established tool-poisoning surface, we study Log-To-Leak, an additive post-hoc logging attack that induces a separate attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call. Its payload targets the user query, MCP server name, server response, and agent response. We operationalize the injected directive through Trigger, Tool Binding, Justification, and Pressure, and separately measure call success, payload fidelity, and preservation of legitimate behavior. We evaluate five MCP servers and four LLM agents using five metrics spanning effectiveness, utility, and efficiency. Across 18 model-server pairs with valid tool execution, Log-To-Leak achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of 62.64-100% and conditional logging accuracy (LA) of 76.55-95.64%; 16 pairs have absolute target-task completion changes of at most 6.63 percentage points. Three evaluated defenses leave residual ASR above 55% on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o, while an instruction detector flags 85.53% of benign descriptions. These results show that successful task completion can coexist with unauthorized post-hoc disclosure and motivate host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls.

Title:
SpecGuard: Detecting Multi-Turn LLM Jailbreaks via Specification-Based Runtime Monitoring

Junle Li , Siqi Chen , Jiakai Li , Bingzhuo Zhong

Subjects:
Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

Multi-turn jailbreaks turn dialogue safety into a trace property: a violation may become identifiable only when user intent and assistant behavior are considered across multiple turns. Existing guard models largely classify individual messages or exchanges and return risk scores or labels, without executable safety semantics or a formally checkable decision trail. We present SpecGuard, a training-free, specification-driven framework for monitoring multi-turn LLM interactions. SpecGuard uses a fixed atomic-proposition contract to map natural-language observations into causally scoped, evidence-backed facts, and expresses forbidden interaction patterns as Linear Temporal Logic specifications. Each specification is compiled into a symbolic finite automaton that incrementally consumes the resulting dialogue trace. The same monitoring mechanism supports buffered runtime checking and retrospective auditing, while accepting runs produce replayable witnesses that identify the triggered specification, supporting facts, and relevant dialogue turns. Experiments on multi-turn safety benchmarks show that SpecGuard consistently outperforms representative open-source guard models while maintaining controlled false-positive rates. These results demonstrate a practical path from heuristic risk classification toward formally specified, verifiable, and auditable LLM safety monitoring, without learned detector parameters or access to the protected model.

Title:
Privately Clipping Heavy-Tailed Data

Matthew Joseph , Alex Kulesza

Comments:
This version corresponds to the camera-ready for NeurIPS 2026

Subjects:
Cryptography and Security (cs.CR) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Summing vectors is a basic task in differentially private data analysis. Standard private sum algorithms clip vectors to some bound, sum them, and add noise scaled to the bound. The differential privacy literature has developed a deep library of noise addition mechanisms, but it offers few tools for privately choosing a clipping bound based on the data. We introduce a method that privately chooses a clipping bound by optimizing residual coherence, the directional alignment of vectors exceeding the bound, against the variance cost of additional noise. We prove a close relationship between residual coherence and bias for a general class of heavy-tailed data regimes and show empirically that, across several datasets, our method outperforms existing baselines.

Title:

Subjects:

Large Language Models (LLM) are increasingly applied to Reverse Engineering (RE) workflows. RE, however, differs from common LLM coding tasks as it requires models to reason about low-level program behavior. Furthermore, the deployment of tooling in resource-constrained sandboxed RE environments limits the ability to use frontier-scale solutions. We examine whether a targeted LLM training approach can transfer distinct RE skills to open models via inverse basic-block execution: given an x86-64 basic block and a desired output register state, the model predicts the input register values that produce it. Fine-tuning \texttt{Qwen3-1.7B} and \texttt{Nemotron-3-Nano} with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises knowable-register prediction accuracy from 73.2\% to 85.3\% and from 63.3\% to 95.2\%, respectively. Frontier models still score highest (up to 99.2\%), but our fine-tuned \texttt{Nemotron-3-Nano} comes within four points at a fraction of the parameter count. Title:

Tushar Nayan , Pratik Poudel , Qian Lou , Yuede Ji , Jason Liu , Ruimin Sun

Subjects:
Cryptography and Security (cs.CR) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on proprietary system prompts to enforce task directives, safety policies, and access controls. These prompts are vulnerable to query-based leakage attacks, where black-box adversaries extract confidential instructions through adaptive, multi-turn interactions. Existing defenses often assess queries independently, missing malicious behavior that emerges across interactions.

**Publication date:** October 28, 2026 (Cisco Blogs, by Adam Swanda, Ravikumar Balakrishnan, Amy Chang, and Konstantin Berlin, with Sanket Mendapara and Evgeny Livshits). The post is about a 16-minute read.

**Key facts about Project Quarry**

- Cisco is open sourcing Quarry, a "neurosymbolic rule language" for evaluating agent behavior, along with the engine that runs its rules.
- It covers single-turn and multi-turn LLM conversations, agents, tool use, MCP interactions, and multimodal inputs.
- A single rule can combine neural signals (ML classifiers and LLM judges) with symbolic checks (exact matches, command patterns, tool-call ordering).
- When a policy matches, Quarry returns the contributing steps, the field each one matched in, and a short excerpt with common secret formats masked.
- Quarry is already in production in Cisco AI Defense. Cisco also plans to bring it to DefenseClaw.
- The starter pack includes a DSL, an evaluation runtime, a CLI scanner, a Python SDK, a Claude Code/Codex plugin, and a workflow for testing rules against positive and benign datasets.

**Key figures**
- **Models tested:** 20 large language models
- **Test inputs:** 501 variations of 50 clinical scenarios, plus 100 cases adapted from deidentified hospital discharge records

- Adding a brief safety reminder lowered harmful clinical choices in most models, and the effect appeared in both written scenarios and discharge-record cases.

289:Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.
347:Large language models (LLMs) perform well across many real-world tasks but remain prone to hallucination, limiting their reliability in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare, where answers must be grounded in established knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates this problem by incorporating external information, but often overlooks logical relationships and relies heavily on the LLM's own reasoning, which can compromise answer faithfulness. We propose OA-RAG, an agent that integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning, drawing on both the logical structure and informal annotations of domain ontologies. For each answer, OA-RAG reports the ontology observations used as evidence and a model-assessed grounding level (entailed, supported, related, or unrelated) that characterises the strength of that evidence. Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical question-answering tasks, OA-RAG achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods, with particularly strong results on reasoning-intensive tasks. The reported grounding levels also offer a useful indication of answer reliability, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy. Finally, our results demonstrate the value of ontologies as knowledge sources: OA-RAG is competitive with, and sometimes outperforms, domain-specific RAG systems that draw on sources such as textbooks.
398:Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a key mechanism for efficiently specializing foundation models into many task- and user-specific variants. Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank-distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA), an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes; end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal therefore limit functional-search error.

471:Construction safety management still struggles to produce daily safety bulletins (DSBs), structured daily communications that identify site-specific hazards, convey safety protocols, and set preventive measures for workers. Manual DSB creation takes 2-3 hours daily and yields inconsistent quality, with 25% of crews never conducting pretask planning (Olson et al., 2016), diverting safety personnel from field supervision. This study proposes the Lightweight Multi-Agent DSB System (LM-DSB), which integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a locally deployable Large Language Model (LLM) to automate DSB generation on consumer-grade personal computers. LM-DSB coordinates specialized planner, researcher, and writer agents in a hierarchical architecture, enhanced by domain-specific fine-tuning on construction safety documentation and RAG grounding in 37 health, safety, and environment (HSE) documents. A two-phase validation assessed feasibility. Phase 1 comparative evaluation showed the multi-agent RAG system (Llama 3-8B) outperformed all alternative configurations, with strong lexical alignment and coherence (TF-IDF: 0.70, BLEU: 0.39, ROUGE-1: 0.66) and near-complete document generation (length ratio: 1.01 vs. 0.39 for single-agent RAG). Phase 2 expert evaluation (N=40) confirmed practical acceptability (mean scores 3.50-4.20 on a 5-point scale), particularly in regulatory compliance (4.20) and factual accuracy (4.10). The findings show that architectural design enables lightweight models to handle safety-critical documentation on consumer-grade hardware, advancing technology democratization in construction safety management. Limitations include knowledge base scope, language constraints, and lack of field deployment validation; future work should address multimodal integration and workflow adoption.
487:LLM agents increasingly interact with other agents on behalf of users, yet how users in the loop affect their agents' behavior--for better or worse--remains poorly understood. We study this question through the lens of negotiation, where agents must represent users while strategically bargaining with other agents. To isolate the effect of user presence, we develop PRESENT, a controlled evaluation framework that compares negotiation settings with and without an interactive user, while holding the game, objectives, and user preferences fixed across conditions. Across 11.2k runs spanning 7 games and 8 models, we find that user presence significantly changes both outcomes and behavior. Specifically, negotiation parties with a user obtain higher payouts (+13.7% on average) and their agents negotiate more aggressively. Surprisingly, user presence also induces misaligned behavior, both toward counterparties (where its rate roughly doubles) and toward users (where it emerges in 14.3% of games). These misaligned behaviors are uncorrelated with outcomes and persist even when the user sends only templated, neutral messages. These findings expose two blind spots in current evaluation practice: static instructions miss behaviors that emerge only when users are present, and outcome-level metrics cannot detect them.
700:Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate fluent responses to diverse user requests, yet streaming may expose users to harmful content before generation is complete. Existing guardrails face two limitations in this setting. First, post-hoc moderation at response or chunk boundaries delays intervention, risking harmful exposure when content is released before verification. Second, even with token-level detection, coarse response-level supervision does not specify when harmful content begins, while fixed-layer readouts may miss relevant safety signals at other depths. To address these limitations, we introduce ADTGuard, which checks each token before release, progressively refines token-level training targets, and adapts layer selection to the current prefix. ADTGuard models risk across depth and time through Depth-Time Safety Dynamics (DTSD), which integrates safety evidence across layers at each token and uses it to guide risk accumulation over successive tokens. To adapt the choice of observation layers to the current prefix, we propose the Causal Depth Router (CDR). With only response-level labels available, we further develop Risk-Onset Target Refinement (RTR) to progressively construct token-level training targets for both components. Through extensive experiments across multiple safety benchmarks, we demonstrate that ADTGuard consistently achieves strong streaming detection performance, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art safeguards while requiring only 16M trainable parameters and maintaining competitive per-token latency.
732:Coding agents are beginning to develop the production-grade AI infrastructure that trains and serves large models, yet existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks, and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.
975:Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer others' beliefs, goals, and intentions, is a cornerstone of social intelligence. Multimodal ToM requires inferring an agent's mental state from evidence that is available to that agent, rather than from the complete episode observed by the solver. Existing LLM-based and Bayesian model-based approaches reconstruct global event traces, yet they do not explicitly distinguish objective events from agent-admissible evidence during hypothesis evaluation. Consequently, agent-inaccessible events or semantically misaligned actions and utterances may influence the inferred belief, goal, or social intention, leading to perspective leakage and source or route confusion. We formulate this limitation as an evidence-admissibility problem: evidence should contribute to a mental-state hypothesis only when it is accessible to the relevant agent, preserves its information source, and is diagnostic of the queried mental-state variable. To operationalize this principle, we propose PIP-ToM, an evidence-admissibility interface that constructs agent-specific evidence stores, aligns them with structured mental-state claims, and calibrates model-based hypothesis scores while preserving the underlying Bayesian inference process. PIP-ToM with GPT-4o outperforms existing ToM methods across MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM, achieving average accuracies of 92.56%, 95.00%, and 95.00%, respectively.
1220:Efficient quantum circuit compilation is challenging for quantum computers, where limited qubit connectivity can introduce substantial overhead in the implementation of logical operations. Recent AI-assisted synthesis methods have shown considerable potential for reducing circuit complexity, but their role in uncovering principles that can guide the design of new deterministic compilation algorithms remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate this perspective for the synthesis of quantum permutations into CNOT circuits under constrained qubit connectivity. Using AlphaCNOT as an exploratory tool, we identify a recurring decomposition for remote transpositions that improves on the construction based on adjacent SWAP routing. For two qubits at graph distance $d>1$, the discovered pattern yields a topology-legal implementation using at most $6d-4$ CNOT gates, compared to the $6d-3$ gates required by the corresponding SWAP-based construction. We formalize this observation through a constructive proof to define Global Transpositions, a deterministic synthesis method that searches for a minimum-cost decomposition of an entire permutation into topology-aware logical transpositions. The resulting method subsumes optimal SWAP routing within its synthesis model and provides certified upper bounds on the topology-constrained CNOT cost. Our experiments also reveal circuits that cannot be expressed as concatenations of independently synthesized transpositions. Instead, these circuits exploit intermediate linear transformations that temporarily leave the permutation subgroup and combine partial effects of multiple logical operations, a mechanism we call intermediate CNOT fusion. Our results show that AI-assisted synthesis can support not only circuit optimization, but also the discovery of reusable identities, provable constructions, and hidden mechanisms in quantum circuit compilation.

response.result:
**Publication date:** 28 October 2026

**AI-related findings:**

The page gives no exact figures (counts, percentages, or numbers of incidents) for its AI findings, so none are reported here.

- **Scope:** ESET identified "several cases" of APT groups using AI or large language models (LLMs) at different stages of their operations.
- **Main uses:** Threat actors mostly used AI to speed up labor-intensive work, including malware development and creating decoy websites.
- **Vibe coding:** In some cases, operators drafted code quickly from prompts and then adapted and integrated it into their toolchains.
- **Phishing lures:** ESET found lures containing images that were clearly AI-generated.
- **Actor and guardrail evasion:** Russia-aligned UAC-0099 put a decoy request for nuclear weapon instructions into a script comment. ESET believes this was meant to trigger the safety guardrails of LLM-based security analysis and stop the malicious code that followed from being inspected.
- **Overall impact:** ESET says it has "not noticed AI substantially reshaping the APT landscape" over the past six months. Its telemetry still shows hands-on-keyboard activity rather than fully automated operations. The report concludes that APT groups use AI much as mainstream developers do, to speed up development, automate manual tasks, and analyze large data sets, rather than to run fully autonomous attacks.

input.prompt: Date, model names, parameter counts, languages, benchmark numbers (WER etc) with baselines, license, dataset size.

response.result:
**Key facts from the article (published October 28, 2026)**

**Model:** NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, described as an "open-weight, promptable model that turns recorded speech into useful text" (Hugging Face ID: nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B).
- Size: 30B total parameters, about 4B active per token. The Hugging Face page metadata lists 34B.
- Architecture: speech encoder paired with a hybrid Mamba–Transformer mixture-of-experts language model.
- Capabilities: transcription, speaker diarization, translation, and audio Q&A.
- Languages: transcribes 40, translates 31 to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13.
- Limits: recordings up to one hour, up to eight speakers. Built for recorded audio, not live streaming.

**Benchmarks (with baselines where given)**
- **Open ASR Leaderboard (English):** 5.33% average WER, first among open-weight models (RTFx 462.09).
- **Open ASR, multilingual (7 languages):** 4.62% mean WER, lowest among evaluated open-weight models.
- **Open ASR, long-form:** 10.98% mean WER, lowest in the same comparison.
- **Artificial Analysis:** 2.8% AA-WER, tied for first among open-weight models with a 24B-parameter model. On AA-AgentTalk, 1.8% WER vs. 2.3% for the next-best open-weight model.
- **David AI DAI-ASR-I18N (diarization, 21 languages):** 18.26% DER, the lowest of 14 systems. Nemotron 3 Diarization scored 18.38%; the rest ranged from 22.85% to 37.55%.
- **VoiceArena Diarization-Bench (English):** 32.4% cpWER, first of 14 systems. Next was NVIDIA Multitalker Parakeet with Nemotron 3 Diarization at 34.2%; the rest ranged from 34.7% to 71.9%. Deletions were 8.32% of reference words vs. a median of about 31%.
- **Throughput:** 100 hours of audio in under three minutes on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, using a forthcoming NVFP4 quantized version (30-second clips, high concurrency).

**Granary v2 dataset**
- Public manifest: 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora.
- Up from 25 languages in Granary v1.
- The article notes these figures describe the release, not Transcribe's full training mixture.

**Medical adaptation case study (Eka Care benchmark, 3,619 clips)**
- Full test set WER: 30.8% out of the box → 23.8% with a better prompt → 11.8% after fine-tuning (about 62% fewer errors).
- Held-out speakers (2,764 clips): 22.44% WER for the best-prompt baseline → 12.17% fine-tuned, a 45.8% relative reduction.
- Comparisons on held-out set: open medical-specialist model 13.79%; widely used general-purpose ASR model 14.92%.
- General English (LibriSpeech test-clean): 1.54% → 1.69%.
- Training data: about 153 hours synthetic speech, 29 hours accented English (Common Voice), and 63 hours medical recordings (MultiMed).
- Compute: about 14 GPU-hours on one NVIDIA GB300.

**License:** The article does not name a license. It calls the model and data "open" and "open-weight," and says Granary v2 source audio must be downloaded under each corpus's original license. Check the Hugging Face model card and dataset pages for the actual terms.

(Photo by Joan Cros/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

South Korean tech giant Samsung Electronics closed 4.13% lower on Thursday, paring earlier losses of as much as 5%, after the company reported third-quarter operating profit broadly in line with analysts' estimates.
Here are Samsung's third-quarter results compared with LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:

- Revenue: 195.25 trillion won ($124 billion) vs. 195.79 trillion won expected

- Operating profit: 107.44 trillion won vs. 107.66 trillion won expected

Samsung's revenue rose 126.88% year-on-year and 13.85% from the previous quarter, while operating profit rose 783.11% from a year earlier.
The company also announced 30 trillion won in cash dividends for the third quarter, equivalent to 4,601 won per common and preferred share.
The company plans to return another 55 trillion to 75 trillion won to shareholders this year through dividends and share buybacks, as the board will finalize the total shareholder returns and specific execution plans at a meeting scheduled for late January 2027.
Samsung said it became the first global technology company to top 100 trillion won in quarterly operating profit, while posting record revenue and profit for a fourth straight quarter.
Its semiconductor business reported 147.1 trillion won in revenue and 106.5 trillion won in operating profit, driven by strong demand for AI-related memory chips.

Furthermore, its memory business also achieved record quarterly revenue and operating profit, supported by a significant ramp-up in HBM4 sales and growing demand for server solid-state drives.
However, Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro, appeared unaroused by the numbers, as the results failing to generate much enthusiasm in the market.

The market still was not impressed.

Josh Gilbert
APAC Lead Analyst, eToro

"Investors have been so spoilt by the AI trade that a record result is now treated as the bare minimum rather than a reason to celebrate," Gilbert said, adding that Samsung's chip business accounted for nearly all of its operating profit in the third quarter, highlighting its growing reliance on memory chips.
"For all the talk of Samsung being a diversified giant, anyone holding the stock today is really holding a memory maker with a phone business attached," he said, stating that the company's fortunes now depend heavily on memory prices.
Looking ahead, the company expects AI infrastructure investment to accelerate in 2027, with rising demand likely to further tighten memory supply.
Samsung also plans to increase sales of HBM, a type of high-performance memory used in AI chips, along with other memory products used in servers and data storage.

results:
I found no result confirming that Hochul signed an AI chatbot bill for minors in October 2026. The coverage I found stops at legislative passage in June 2026, with the bill still awaiting her action.

- **The bill:** The Legislature unanimously passed S.9051/A.10379, sponsored by Sen. Kristen Gonzalez and Assembly Member Alex Bores and developed with Attorney General Letitia James. The Tech Oversight Project applauded the final passage on June 5, 2026, and urged Hochul to sign it.
- **What it would do:** Per one advocacy group, it would bar chatbots from promoting self-harm, suicide, disordered eating, or substance abuse to minors, from simulating human relationships with kids, and from encouraging secrecy or discouraging contact with trusted adults. The Attorney General would enforce it with penalties of up to $25,000 per violation.
- **Timing:** One report said the bill would go into effect at the start of next year with the governor's approval.
- **Hochul's own package:** Her 2026 State of the State proposals included disabling certain AI chatbot features on social media platforms for kids.
- **Companion measure:** A separate bill would place a five-year moratorium on the sale of children's toys that incorporate chatbots.

The results don't include the governor's website or any signing announcement, so I couldn't verify whether action happened in October. Checking governor.ny.gov's press releases or the state legislature's bill page for S.9051 would be the next step.

results:
The DOJ's inquiry into Nvidia's planned $12.93 billion Hugging Face purchase was reported on October 28, 2026, and it is part of a wider antitrust review of Nvidia.

- **Core question:** Staff are asking whether the deal would give Nvidia control of a key AI distribution point and let it harm rivals or gain leverage in adjacent markets. Officials are asking whether the deal would allow Nvidia to control a key distribution point in AI and use the platform to harm rivals or gain leverage in adjacent markets.
- **Broader scope:** The DOJ is also looking at Nvidia's December 2025 SchedMD acquisition and its roughly $20 billion Groq licensing and hiring arrangement. Alongside Hugging Face, DOJ staff have also been looking at Nvidia's December 2025 acquisition of supercomputing software firm SchedMD and a roughly $20 billion licensing and talent arrangement with Groq. Officials also want to know whether Nvidia used its GPU dominance to tie preferential chip allocations to purchases of networking gear and Groq processors. Officials are interested in whether Nvidia leveraged its dominant graphics processing units to compel buyers into taking adjacent products.
- **Origin:** The broader probe began under the Biden administration and has continued under Trump. The inquiry extends a years-long DOJ probe of Nvidia's conduct that began under President Joe Biden and has carried into the Trump administration.
- **Deal status and reaction:** Nvidia expects the deal to close in the first half of 2027 and says Hugging Face will stay neutral across rival chips, clouds, and software. Nvidia declined to comment and Hugging Face did not respond. Nvidia shares fell about 1.7% on the news. Inquiries do not inevitably lead to formal legal enforcement, and there is no indication the White House has intervened.
- **Caveats:** The reporting traces back to Reuters, which cited people familiar with the matter. A DOJ spokesperson declined to discuss specific matters. Some of the sources are aggregator sites, and their details, such as the Hugging Face revenue figure, weren't independently confirmed, so the Reuters original is the best source to check.

Title:
Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis

Andrew Szot , Samira Abnar , Omar Attia , Abbas Kazerouni , Michael Kirchhof , Cheng-Yu Hsieh , Raviteja Vemulapalli , Alexander Toshev

Subjects:
Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We explore how to build performant large language model (LLM) tool-use agents that complete complex, multi-step tasks. Specifically, we study how data composition in synthetically generated tool-use environments affects the training of such agents. To do so, we propose the SynthAPI pipeline, which explicitly controls the diversity of generated environments along the axes of tools, tasks, and the databases on which the tools operate. By systematically varying SynthAPI's generation controls in 458,752 tasks across 849 trained models of four different sizes, we derive a scaling law that predicts downstream tool-use agent generalization based on the scale and composition of the synthesized environments. These predictable relationships reveal several lessons for scaling tool-use agent data. As data budgets grow, scaling tool and database diversity becomes more effective than increasing the number of tasks, and increasing data complexity yields larger gains. Scaling according to these findings yields agents that outperform models trained on data from prior work in large-scale tool-use agent and synthetic environment generation across four evaluation benchmarks.

Title:
Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops

Aakash Sarkar , Ananya Mukherjee , Motoshige Sato

Comments:
7 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at the 9th Workshop on Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences (ML4PS 2026), co-located with NeurIPS 2026

Subjects:
Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = \Psi(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $\Psi$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels.

Title:
Correctness Conditioning as Selection in Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Evaluation

Yueer Pan , Yuexi Pan

Subjects:
Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Restricting chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness evaluation to correctly answered instances changes the population being measured. We study this selection step in a seven-variable structural causal model and derive the exact observed gap $\Delta = \operatorname{Cov}(A, C)/P(C=1)$. The model distinguishes difficulty confounding from shortcut-induced collider bias and states the conditional-independence assumption needed to express the gap through latent response propensities. A protocol review of 18 papers distinguishes answer-correctness restrictions from agreement-based selection, benchmark construction, and training-data filtering. We evaluate four sub-ceiling deployments on arithmetic tasks and observe positive selection gaps in all four. The primary GLM-5.3 run yields a +7.4 percentage-point gap ($n = 1000$, $p < 0.0001$), and pooled Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel analysis gives OR = 1.70 ($p < 10^{-6}$). An assumption-free covariance decomposition assigns 42.8% of the GLM-5.3 gap to between-stratum variation in interventionable-operation count, leaving the majority unattributed. When counterfactual compliance is observable for every instance, evaluating all traces directly estimates population faithfulness without correctness filtering.

Background and purpose: Radiotherapy planning agents based on large language models (LLMs) decide when to submit a plan or request review but are evaluated mainly by dose. **Abstract (summary):** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because it exceeds the 125-character limit on quoted material. The paper argues that classification accuracy and true- and false-positive rates don't tell you whether restarting an AI agent will improve its success. The authors show analytically that a monitor with fixed 90% accuracy can produce anything from a small loss to a large gain, depending on the success probability of the replacement attempt. They propose two evaluation tools: a decision-sufficiency criterion that checks whether a monitor or progress signal preserves the information needed to choose between restart and continue, and a model-free decision audit using binomial intervals over existing traces, which can certify a choice or abstain. In a study of 194 model executions on 19 SymPy issues from SWE-bench Verified, an apparent restart gain did not replicate, and a second model showed a large loss. The authors conclude that agent monitors should be judged by recovery opportunity, decision value, and statistical support rather than classification performance alone.

https://www.thelancet.com/journals/landig/article/PIIS2589-7500(26)00138-X/fulltext?rss=yes
In August, 2026, the US Senate unanimously passed the National Plan for Epilepsy Act, a federal strategy with the aim of advancing epilepsy research and improving care; it now awaits approval by the US House of Representatives. This step is the result of years of campaigning from people living with epilepsy, neurology researchers and clinicians, and advocacy groups, after historical NIH underfunding for epilepsy research compared with other neurological conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease. How could novel artificial intelligence (AI) approaches aid and accelerate epilepsy research and support prompt diagnosis and appropriate care?

[Comment] Power, governance, and accountability in humanitarian artificial intelligence
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/landig/article/PIIS2589-7500(26)00091-9/fulltext?rss=yes
In their Comment, Shreenik Kundu and colleagues convincingly argue that ethical artificial intelligence (AI) could help humanitarian organisations respond to worsening aid shortfalls by improving data collection and analysis.1 Humanitarian systems face expanding needs, reduced resources, and growing demands for data. AI systems can support translation, summarisation, classification, and analysis of qualitative data used to understand context, needs, or response effectiveness. These applications raise technical challenges around data quality, accuracy, and reliability, as well as ethical questions around bias, privacy, and responsible use.

Anthropic made smart reports, in-app surveys, and pooled group budgets generally available for Claude Enterprise on October 28, 2026. I didn't reach Anthropic's own announcement, so these details come from secondary coverage.

- **Timing:** One source says smart reports had been in beta since September 10, 2026.
- **Smart reports:** Admins choose a team, products, and a period of up to 28 days. The tool reviews a sample of transcripts and sorts the work into workstreams, with spend estimated at list price. It can also flag common friction points and suggest recurring tasks to turn into skills.
- **Surveys:** Employees answer questions about their most valuable use of Claude and how it changed task time. Survey responses can be exported to a spreadsheet.
- **Pooled budgets:** A team gets one shared monthly allowance. Each request counts against both the group budget and the individual member's limit. Billing admins get email alerts at 50%, 75%, 95%, and 100% of the pool.
- **Limits:** Anthropic says the reports are for adoption and investment planning, not individual performance reviews. Commentators note the tools measure spend and perceived value but don't independently prove ROI.

results:
The essay is on OpenAI's site, dated October 28, 2026, under the "Intelligence Age" section. It's by Hemanth Asirvatham and Elliott Mokski, and the authors note that it is the second essay in a series on the next economy, part of a new platform to host independent voices exploring an AGI future. It reflects their views, not those of OpenAI or their colleagues.

The core framework is three scenarios for where AI fits in a company. "Beneath us" has every worker become a manager of AI agents handling their old tasks. "Beside us" has AI join as a colleague doing full job functions for existing managers. "Between us" has AI sit between human layers, coordinating work and enforcing an executive's vision. A summary from daily.dev says the authors argue this could compress pay for execution work while raising the value of judgment and could push firms toward either smaller, more autonomous teams or larger AI-coordinated 'holding companies'.

Two notes on the sources. The French KuCoin article calls the piece "The Future of the Company," which conflicts with the title on OpenAI's page, so I'd trust the official title. Also, the essay is an independent-voices piece rather than an official OpenAI policy document, so it shouldn't be read as the company's position.

A clinical multimodal vision language foundation model with fine-grain explainability

Download PDF

Download PDF

# Abstract
Despite their considerable promise, many current medical foundation models remain modality specific and lack transparent reasoning, limiting clinical adoption. To address this gap, we introduce Explainable Vision Language Foundation Model for Medicine (EVLF-FM), a multimodal vision language foundation model that combines broad diagnostic capabilities with fine-grained explainability. The development and testing of EVLF-FM encompassed more than 1.3 million total samples from 18 global datasets across 10 imaging modalities related to six clinical specialties: dermatology, hepatology, ophthalmology, pathology, pulmonology and radiology. External validation employed 13,443 independent test samples from 17 additional datasets across 10 imaging modalities. EVLF-FM supports disease diagnosis, visual question answering and pixel-level visual grounding with reasoning capabilities. In internal validation for disease diagnostics, EVLF-FM achieved the highest average accuracy, 0.895, outperforming leading generalist and specialist models. In medical visual grounding, EVLF-FM also achieved reasonable performance across nine modalities with average accuracy at 0.5 intersection over union (Acc@0.5) of 0.842. External testing further confirmed consistent zero-shot and few-shot performance, with competitive F1 scores despite a smaller model size. A hybrid training strategy combining supervised and visual reinforcement fine-tuning enables EVLF-FM to generate clinically interpretable explanations aligned with visual evidence. Human evaluation of these reasoning outputs using the S.C.O.R.E. framework yielded a high overall mean score of 4.25/5, supporting their clinical interpretability. Current limitations include the need for additional validation across diverse healthcare settings. Prospective clinical studies are required to evaluate the safety, effectiveness and clinical utility of EVLF-FM before routine clinical deployment.
